problemText: Which pronoun is in subject case? Think about the pronoun that does the action in a sentence.
choices: them
his
she
me
hints: Subject case pronouns do the verb.
Look for the pronoun that matches 'I, we, he, she, they, who.'

problemText: Read the sentence: 'The coach gave the trophy to Marcus and ___.' Which pronoun belongs in the blank? Use the preposition rule to help you decide.
choices: I
mine
my
me
hints: What preposition comes right before the blank?
Object case always follows a preposition.

problemText: Which sentence uses the possessive pronoun correctly? Remember the rule about apostrophes in possessive pronouns.
choices: That skateboard is theirs, and this one is mine.
The pencil case is her's, not his.
The backpack is their's because it has their initials.
We found the dog but not it's collar.
hints: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe.
Check each choice for an apostrophe on a possessive pronoun like theirs, hers, or its.

problemText: Read the sentence: 'Between you and ___, I think we should help them set up the chairs.' Use the drop test to find the right pronoun. First identify the preposition, then test the pronoun alone in the sentence to see what works.
choices: I
me
my
myself
hints: Drop 'you and' and read just 'Between ___.' What sounds right?
Remember that object case always comes after a preposition.

problemText: Two blanks need pronouns: 'Lexi and ___ finished the project, and the teacher praised Lexi and ___ for it.' The same pair 'Lexi and ___' needs different pronouns in each blank because the jobs are different. What are the two correct pronouns?
choices: I, I
me, me
I, me
me, I
hints: Use the drop test on each blank separately. First blank: '___ finished the project.' Second blank: 'the teacher praised ___.'
In the first blank, the pronoun does the verb finished. In the second blank, the pronoun receives the action of praised.

problemText: Read these three sentences from a text message exchange: (1) 'At the game, Aisha sat with Marcus and ___.' (2) 'Our team played against theirs, and ___ won by three points.' (3) 'The other team's goalie was better than ___.' Identify which blank needs object case, which needs subject case, and which needs possessive case. What are the three correct pronouns in order?
choices: me, they, ours
me, they, me
I, them, their
me, they, him
hints: For blank 1, find the preposition. For blank 2, ask who is doing the verb won. For blank 3, use comparison with the goalie noun to decide if ownership or object case fits.

Blank 1 comes after the preposition 'with,' so it must be object case. Blank 2 does the verb won, so it must be subject case. Blank 3 comes after 'than' (a preposition), so it must be object case, and the pronoun refers to the goalie as a person.

problemText: Which sentence uses an intensive pronoun correctly? Remember: an intensive pronoun adds emphasis to a subject or object that is already named in the same sentence.
choices: Myself and my sister baked cookies together.
Myself baked the cookies.
The cookies and myself were delicious.
I baked the cookies myself.
hints: Look for a sentence where the -self word is emphasizing a subject or object that is already there, not filling a slot on its own.
Try the deletion test: remove the -self word and see if the sentence still makes complete sense with the same subject.

problemText: Read this sentence: 'The coach himself gave us feedback on our performance.' Use the deletion test to determine whether 'himself' is used correctly. What happens when you remove it?
choices: The sentence still reads 'The coach gave us feedback on our performance' with the same meaning, so 'himself' is correctly emphasizing the subject.
The sentence remains complete and makes sense without it, proving 'himself' is not needed to fill a grammatical role and is therefore serving as a reflexive pronoun incorrectly.
The sentence loses all its meaning and cannot function without 'himself' because 'himself' is the only subject performing the action of giving feedback.
The sentence becomes ungrammatical without 'himself' because it is being used as a reflexive pronoun to show that the coach gave feedback to himself rather than to someone else.
hints: An intensive pronoun passes the deletion test—the sentence remains complete and means the same thing without it.
Ask yourself: after you delete the word, is 'the coach' still clearly the subject doing the action?

problemText: Which sentence contains an error in the use of a -self word? Read each one carefully and ask whether the -self word is emphasizing a subject or object that is already there, or whether it is filling a slot on its own.
choices: Maya solved the math problem herself without using a calculator.
My brother and myself went to the store after school.
The two of us ourselves completed the entire project by Friday.
The principal herself cut the ribbon at the grand opening of the new wing.
hints: In a compound subject or object, look to see if a plain pronoun like 'I' or 'me' is also present in that pair.
Try covering up the other name in the pair and reading the -self word alone—does it need to fill the slot by itself?

problemText: Read the sentence: 'The coach and myself watched the game from the sidelines.' This sentence has an error. Use what you learned about the drop test and the deletion test to identify the problem and state the correction.
choices: The error is that 'myself' needs another -self word to pair with it; the sentence should be 'The coach and himself watched the game from the sidelines.'
The error is that 'myself' is being used as a reflexive pronoun instead of an intensive pronoun; the sentence should be 'The coach watched myself from the sidelines.'

The error is that 'myself' is filling the subject slot on its own with no other 'I' present to be emphasized, so the correct subject pronoun is 'I': 'The coach and I watched the game from the sidelines.'
The error is that 'myself' makes the sentence too informal; use 'me' instead: 'The coach and me watched the game from the sidelines.'
hints: Run the deletion test: what happens if you remove 'myself'? Does the sentence fall apart, or does it stay complete?
Use the drop test: cover 'the coach and' and read the pronoun alone—does it work as a subject by itself, and if not, what subject pronoun does belong there?

problemText: A student wrote: 'The teacher gave the assignment to my friend and myself.' Identify the error and explain why it is wrong using one of the two tests from the lesson.
choices: The error is that 'myself' is too formal; the sentence should use 'me' but only when standing alone, not in a compound.
The error is that 'myself' is correctly used because it emphasizes the object; the sentence should stay exactly as written.
The error is that 'myself' cannot follow a preposition; the sentence should use 'I' instead: 'gave the assignment to my friend and I.'

The error is that 'myself' is filling the object slot after the preposition 'to' on its own, with no other 'me' in the sentence for it to emphasize; when you remove 'myself' and read 'gave the assignment to,' the sentence is incomplete because an object pronoun is needed.
hints: An intensive pronoun repeats a subject or object that is already in the sentence; look for another 'I' or 'me' somewhere else for 'myself' to be emphasizing.
The deletion test shows that the sentence breaks without the -self word, which proves it was never adding emphasis—it was standing in the slot by itself.

problemText: A classmate wrote two sentences in a story: 'Sarah and myself went to the beach. We built a sandcastle, and I decorated it myself.' Which sentence has an error, which is correct, and what is the one key difference that makes one right and one wrong?
choices: The first sentence is wrong because 'myself' is filling the subject slot in the compound with no other 'I' present, but the second sentence is correct because 'myself' emphasizes 'I,' which is already named as the subject earlier in the sentence.

The first sentence is correct because 'myself' adds emphasis to the entire compound subject 'Sarah and myself,' but the second sentence is wrong because using -self words in the middle of a sentence makes writing unclear and confusing.
Both sentences are wrong because -self words should never appear in stories or narrative writing, and they only belong in formal academic papers and business documents.
Both sentences are correct because 'myself' is an acceptable pronoun choice in both compound subjects and object positions when writers want to add emphasis and formality.
hints: In the second sentence, ask yourself: is there another 'I' named somewhere else in that sentence that 'myself' could be emphasizing?
For the first sentence, run the deletion test mentally: if you removed 'myself' from 'Sarah and __ went to the beach,' what subject pronoun would you need to fill that blank?

problemText: What does it mean for pronouns to be consistent in a piece of writing? Explain using the two parts that have to match throughout.
choices: The pronoun's person and number must stay the same from the beginning of the piece to the end, unless the writing gives a real reason for them to change.
The pronouns must be spelled correctly and refer back to the same person each time they are used, with no switches between singular and plural forms allowed.
A pronoun is consistent when it stays in the same grammatical tense as the verb it describes and does not shift between past and present action.
Pronouns are consistent if the piece maintains one voice throughout, meaning all pronouns must follow the rules of formal writing by avoiding contractions and informal speech patterns.
hints: Think about the two vocabulary words from the lesson: person and number. Both of these have to stay steady.
The lesson said 'EVERY PIECE OF WRITING SETS A PERSON AND A NUMBER FOR ITS STORY, AND BOTH HAVE TO HOLD FOR THE WHOLE PIECE.' What has to hold steady?

problemText: Read this passage: 'I made a smoothie for breakfast this morning. You blend the frozen berries with yogurt until it is thick and creamy. Then I added a handful of granola on top.' Which sentence contains the pronoun that does not match the rest of the passage, and what should it be changed to?
choices: The second sentence should change 'You' to 'we' because the passage talks about making something together.
The second sentence should change 'You' to 'I' because the passage is about only one person making a smoothie.
The third sentence should change 'I' to 'you' because the passage is giving instructions to the reader.
The first sentence should change 'I' to 'you' because breakfast is something everyone eats.
hints: Hold the pronoun from the first sentence in your mind. Is it first person or second person? Now check the second sentence. Does it match?
The passage opens with 'I' and nobody new is introduced. The passage is not speaking to a reader. So what pronoun should the second sentence use?

problemText: A student wrote: 'My best friend and I entered the talent show together. We practiced our dance routine for three weeks straight. I added special lighting effects that made the stage glow during our performance.' Is there a pronoun shift in this passage? Why or why not?
choices: Yes, there is a shift from plural to singular, which is always wrong in a piece of writing.
Yes, there is a shift. The passage should say 'we added special lighting effects' because the same people did everything together.
No, there is no shift. The passage opens with 'I' and 'my friend' together (we), and 'I' later marks a solo task the passage explains.
No, because all three sentences use the same pronouns and nothing changes.
hints: The lesson said a shift is only a mistake if the writing did NOT give a real reason for the pronoun to change. Did this passage explain why one person was doing something alone?
Look for what changed in the story, not just what changed in the pronouns. Did the task change? Did the group get smaller?

problemText: Read this passage: 'My brother and I painted the fence in the backyard on Saturday. We mixed the paint and poured it into the roller tray. I painted the left side while my brother painted the right side. By the end of the day, we high-fived because it was finished.' The passage uses both 'I' and 'we.' Explain whether this is a pronoun shift that needs fixing, and tell what rule from the lesson you used to decide.
choices: This is a shift that needs fixing because the passage switches between 'I' and 'we' too many times, violating the lesson's rule that you must pick one pronoun at the start and never change it under any circumstance.
This is a shift that needs fixing because a piece of writing should never switch between 'I' and 'we' no matter what happens in the story or how the tasks are divided.
This is a shift that needs fixing because the passage should stay in 'I' the whole time since one person is the main narrator telling the story.

This is not a shift that needs fixing because the passage explains real reasons for the pronouns to change. The 'I' marks one person's solo task (painting one side), and 'we' returns when both were working together again (high-fiving about the finished job).
hints: The lesson said: 'NOT EVERY CHANGE IS A MISTAKE — CHECK WHETHER SOMETHING REAL CHANGED FIRST.' Did something real change in this passage? Did the group doing the task change?
The rule says to ask: 'Did the writing introduce a reason for this pronoun to be different, or did it just slide?' What reason does this passage give for the pronouns to change?

problemText: A student is fixing this passage: 'I saved money all summer by walking dogs in the neighborhood. By August, I had enough to buy a used skateboard. You can customize it with new grip tape and wheels, which I did right away. Now I show it off at the skate park every day.' The student sees a problem in the third sentence and must decide what to change. What is the correct fix, and why does it work?
choices: Change 'You' to 'I' in the third sentence because the passage is about one person's experience, not instructions for a reader.
Change 'I' to 'you' in the fourth sentence so the whole passage speaks to the reader instead of mixing up who is talking.
Delete the word 'You' from the third sentence and rewrite the whole passage in third person to avoid confusion.
Change 'skateboard' to 'skateboards' in the second sentence so that 'you' and 'I' both refer to plural objects.
hints: The passage opens in first person singular ('I'). When you find a pronoun that does not match, change only THAT pronoun, not the whole passage.
Who is the passage actually about? Is it giving instructions to a reader, or telling about one person's summer? What pronoun should fit from start to finish?

problemText: Read this passage: 'My cousin and I decided to build a treehouse together last spring. We gathered wood and nails from the garage. We climbed into the oak tree with our supplies. Once we were up there, I hammered the boards while you held them steady. By sunset, we had built a frame that would hold our weight.' Find all the pronouns that do not match the person and number set at the opening of the passage. Which pronouns need to be fixed, and what should they be changed to? Explain your reasoning.
choices: Change 'we' in the last sentence to 'I' because the passage should stick to singular pronouns once any task is split between people doing different parts of the work.

Change 'you' to 'my cousin' because the passage opens about two people working together, but no reader is present. The passage never introduces a second person to address, so 'you' has nobody real to point at.

Change only 'I' to 'we' in the fourth sentence because the passage is telling a story from the perspective of two builders, and that sentence breaks the shared perspective even though the work continued to involve both people.
Change both 'I' and 'we' to 'my cousin and I' because mixing pronouns in different numbers makes the passage unclear and confusing to readers who are trying to follow the story.
hints: Read the whole passage and list who is actually in it. Are there two people building together, or is a reader present too? What does the passage tell you?

The lesson said that if a pronoun like 'you' or 'we' has no real person to point at in the passage, it is a shift with no reason. Does this passage ever speak directly to a reader or introduce a third person?

problemText: Which sentence contains a double negative that needs to be revised for standard English?
choices: I do not have any pencils left.
She didn't bring nothing to the meeting.
They were not ready for the test.
He does not like the new rule.
hints: A double negative means two negative words in the same clause.
Look for 'not' or 'don't' paired with 'no,' 'nothing,' or 'nobody.'

problemText: A student wrote this sentence in a science report: 'The experiment ain't shown the results we expected.' Which revision uses the exact standard verb form that fits this sentence?
choices: The experiment is not shown the results we expected.
The experiment was not shown the results we expected.
The experiment has not shown the results we expected.
The experiment does not shown the results we expected.
hints: Ask yourself: what helper verb works with 'shown'? Is it about the past or the present?
'Ain't' can mean am not, is not, are not, has not, or have not—pick the one that matches the action described.

problemText: Read this sentence from a draft: 'They doesn't want to stay late after school.' Which change fixes the subject-verb mismatch in this sentence?
choices: Change 'they' to 'he.'
Change 'want' to 'wants.'
Change 'to stay' to 'stay.'
Change 'doesn't' to 'don't.'
hints: The subject is 'they,' which is plural. What verb form goes with a plural subject?
Standard English pairs 'they' with 'do not' or 'don't,' not 'does not' or 'doesn't.'

problemText: A caption for a yearbook photo reads: 'We wasn't expecting the surprise, and nobody didn't yell louder than the team captains.' Rewrite this sentence so it follows standard English for formal print without changing its meaning.
choices: We were not expecting the surprise, and nobody yelled louder than the team captains.
We weren't expecting the surprise, and nobody didn't yell louder than the team captains.
We were expecting the surprise, and nobody clapped louder than the team captains.
We wasn't expecting the surprise, and nobody yelled louder than the team captains.
hints: Look for two kinds of errors: a subject-verb mismatch and a double negative in the second half.
When you fix 'wasn't' for the plural subject 'we,' and when you fix the two negative words 'nobody' and 'didn't,' does the sentence still mean the same thing?

problemText: A student's draft says: 'The coach ain't never given up on this team, and she don't accept no excuses.' Which sentence revises both errors correctly and keeps the same meaning?
choices: The coach is not never giving up on this team, and she don't accept any excuses.
The coach has never given up on this team, and she does not accept any excuses.
The coach isn't ever giving up on this team, and she doesn't accept no excuses.
The coach has never given up on this team, and she do not accept excuses.
hints: One sentence uses 'ain't' with 'given'—what helper verb works with the past-tense form 'given'?
The second half has 'don't' with a singular subject 'coach,' which needs a different form, plus a double negative with 'accept' and 'no.'

problemText: A student is writing a formal letter to the school principal. The draft contains three sentences: (1) 'I ain't received my report card yet.' (2) 'The office don't have my address on file.' (3) 'They can't find nothing in the system.' The student wants to revise all three for standard English. Which set of revisions is correct and keeps each sentence's original meaning intact?
choices: I haven't never received my report card yet. The office does not has my address on file. They cannot find no information in the system.
I am not received my report card yet. The office is not having my address on file. They can't find nothing in the system.
I have not received my report card yet. The office does not have my address on file. They cannot find anything in the system.
I have not been receiving my report card yet. The office don't have my address on file no longer. They can't find nothing there anymore.
hints: For each sentence, identify whether the error is 'ain't,' a subject-verb mismatch, a double negative, or a combination.
After you revise, reread all three sentences together—does the letter still say the same thing it did before, or did the meaning change?
